title: If You See Earthworms After Rain, Your Garden Is conveying some kind of message
fullText: Do you also hate seeing worms all over your backyard and sidewalks after a rainstorm? Dirty, slimy, creepy. Most people either walk around them or crush them without a second thought. But here's a fact you probably don't know. Every worm you kill is a small loss for your lawn. Some estimates suggest that replacing the work earthworms do naturally can cost homeowners anywhere from hundreds to thousands of dollars a year in fertilizers and soil treatments. For years, I believed the same thing most people do. Rain floods the soil. Worms crawl out. End of story. But the deeper I looked into it, the stranger it became. Because many of those worms weren't escaping. They were traveling. Watch until the end because I'll show you one simple thing you can do that can turn these slimy pests into pure gold for your garden. After a heavy rain, you've probably seen a scene like this. Dozens, hundreds, sometimes thousands of earthworms wriggling across concrete. Their bodies covered in mucus. No eyes, no legs, just twisting and crawling across a landscape they were never meant to cross. Your first reaction is probably gross. Children reach down to touch them. Adults quickly pull them away. Don't touch that. It's dirty. And at that moment, almost everyone arrives at the same conclusion. The rain flooded their tunnels, so they're escaping before they drown. It sounds logical. It feels obvious, and it's wrong. The real story turns out to be much more complicated, because earthworms don't have lungs. None. Which means drowning isn't the death sentence most people think it is. In fact, some earthworm species can tolerate surprisingly long periods in saturated soil or even standing water. Some even tolerate flooded soil surprisingly well. So if they're not escaping from drowning, why are they risking their lives to come above ground? The answer is fascinating. When rain falls, the world transforms. The ground becomes a giant biological highway. Normally moving through soil requires enormous effort. Every inch must be pushed through, tunnneled through, carved out. But after rain, the surface becomes slick and wet. A journey that might have taken hours underground can suddenly be completed in minutes. They're not fleeing. They're traveling. Searching for new territory, searching for mates. Imagine being trapped your entire life inside a few square meters of underground tunnels. Then suddenly one day the entire neighborhood becomes accessible. That's what rain means to an earthworm. It's an opportunity, a rare chance to expand their world. So those worms you see desperately writhing across the sidewalk, they're not panicking. They're sprinting. They don't know death is waiting ahead. They don't know the concrete will confuse them. They don't know the morning sun can dry them out in less than an hour. They only know one thing. This is the biggest opportunity of their lives. And tragically, that's often when we become their executioners. But before we continue, you need to understand what these tiny creatures actually mean for the soil beneath your feet. Because without earthworms, entire ecosystems would struggle to function. Charles Darwin spent nearly 40 years studying earthworms. In the final book he published during his lifetime, he wrote that it may be doubted whether there are many other animals that have played so important a part in the history of the world as these lowly organized creatures. That's a remarkable statement. But why did Darwin think they were so important? Because earthworms are among nature's greatest engineers. Every day they consume dead leaves, decaying roots, and organic debris. But the real magic happens inside their digestive system. Their gut functions like a biological recycling plant. Materials that plants can't directly use are broken down by complex communities of microbes. What comes out the other end is known as vermiccast. Some gardeners value worm castings so highly that they jokingly compare them to buried treasure. Compared to ordinary soil, earthworm castings typically contain dramatically higher levels of plant available nutrients. Compared with ordinary soil, worm castings often contain higher concentrations of several nutrients that plants rely on, including nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. But vermiccast isn't just fertilizer. It's a living soil amendment packed with beneficial microorganisms. And that's only half the story. As earthworms move through the ground, they create an enormous network of tunnels. These tunnels allow roots to breathe. They allow rain water to penetrate deep into the soil instead of pooling on the surface. They improve drainage. They reduce compaction. They create pathways for microbial life to thrive. In other words, earthworms are working around the clock as your lawn's unpaid maintenance crew. a living fertilizer factory operating 24 hours a day and they never send you a bill. So if they're so valuable, why do so many end up dying on sidewalks? Because on concrete they're effectively blind and lost. Earthworms navigate the world through subtle environmental cues, tiny vibrations, moisture gradients, changes in soil texture. A healthy patch of earth constantly feeds them information. information that helps them understand where they are and where they should go. But concrete provides none of those signals. Imagine being dropped into an endless desert with no map, no landmarks, and no sense of direction. That's what a sidewalk feels like to an earthworm. They keep moving, keep searching, and become increasingly disoriented. Then the rain stops, the puddles evaporate, the sun comes out, and that's when the real danger begins. Earthworms breathe through their skin. To survive, that skin must stay moist. As their bodies lose water, critical biological functions begin to fail. The drying process can happen shockingly fast, especially on hot pavement. What looks like frantic dancing is often the final struggle of an animal slowly dehydrating under the sun. And that's the tragedy. Earthworms evolved for more than 400 million years. They learned how to survive underground, how to avoid predators, how to find food, how to find mates in complete darkness. But evolution never prepared them for asphalt roads and concrete sidewalks. They're not being hunted. They're being stranded in a world they were never designed to understand. Now for the good news. Helping them is incredibly easy. The bad news, most people accidentally do it wrong. The most common response is to pick them up with bare hands. That sounds kind, but it's not ideal. Human skin contains salts, oils, and residues that can irritate their extremely sensitive bodies. A much safer approach is simple. Step one, find a leaf, a piece of paper, or even a small stick. Step two, gently lift the worm. Step three, place it in nearby grass, mulch, leaf litter, or soft soil, and then watch. Within seconds, its instincts take over. It disappears back into the earth where it belongs. That tiny action takes only a few seconds, but it may save a creature that will spend the next year improving the soil around your home. Not a bad return on investment. But perhaps the most important thing about earthworms isn't compassion. It's what they can tell you. Because earthworms are also a living diagnostic tool, a health report for your lawn. If [clears throat] you see a handful of worms after a heavy rain, that's perfectly normal. But if you're seeing hundreds or thousands every time it rains, your yard may be trying to tell you something. Here's a simple rule. If the ground remains water logged hours after rainfall, your drainage may be poor. If the soil feels hard and compacted underfoot, your lawn may be suffering from severe compaction. And if unusually large numbers of worms are repeatedly appearing on the surface, those problems may be connected. At that point, the solution isn't more fertilizer, and it isn't pesticides. The solution is healthier soil, better irerration, better drainage, and ironically, earthworms themselves are some of the best natural tools for accomplishing exactly that. Save one earthworm and you're helping preserve countless future plants. Learn to understand what they're telling you and you may prevent serious soil degradation before it becomes visible. That's a connection most people never make, but it's one of the hidden stories unfolding beneath our feet every day. So the next time you see earthworms scattered across a sidewalk after a storm, I hope you don't feel disgust. I hope you see something else. A remarkable survivor, a tiny ecosystem engineer, a creature whose work helps sustain the world around you and perhaps the future health of your own backyard. If this video changed the way you think about earthworms, if it inspired you to look at the natural world with a little more curiosity and a little more compassion, please leave a like. Not just to support the channel, but to honor one of nature's most overlooked architects. And don't forget to subscribe because in the next episode, we'll uncover another hidden secret from the natural world right outside your door. Share this video with your friends and family and help them [clears throat] see these misunderstood creatures through the lens of science instead of instinct. I'm Backyard Story and I'll see you in the next

segments.text: They're being stranded in a world they were never designed to understand.

segments.text: Now for the good news.
segments.viText: Bây giờ là tin tốt.

segments.text: Helping them is incredibly easy.

segments.text: The bad news, most people accidentally do it wrong.
segments.viText: Tin xấu là hầu hết mọi người đều vô tình làm sai.

segments.text: The most common response is to pick them up with bare hands.
segments.viText: Phản ứng phổ biến nhất là nhặt chúng bằng tay không.

segments.text: That sounds kind, but it's not ideal.
segments.viText: Điều đó nghe có vẻ tử tế nhưng nó không lý tưởng chút nào.

segments.text: Human skin contains salts, oils, and residues that can irritate their extremely sensitive bodies.
segments.viText: Da người chứa muối, dầu và cặn có thể gây kích ứng cho cơ thể cực kỳ nhạy cảm của họ.

segments.text: A much safer approach is simple.
segments.viText: Một cách tiếp cận an toàn hơn nhiều rất đơn giản.

segments.viText: Bước hai, nhẹ nhàng nhấc con sâu lên.

segments.viText: Bước ba, đặt nó vào bãi cỏ, lớp phủ, lớp lá rụng hoặc đất mềm gần đó và
